en: Sing me your song, father;
Tell your secret as truly as your faith.
Where is tamarisk-grown Keng-Kol?
He who dwells in Talas—
Where is the warrior Manas?
From the people of the Islamic faith,
Is there a letter you have sought and received?
Your mountain horses are nine multitudes.
Oh, father Akbaltay,
Is there a horse to ride to war?
Father, Khan Baltay, hear my words.
A swift steed to ride to war—
I have searched and cannot find one.
To lion prince Manas,
I shall not rest until I come!”
Before he had finished speaking,
Before he could close his mouth,
That warrior Akbaltay,
Shimmering like flowing mail,
With all his resources still at hand,
Began to speak with a radiant face:
“My Chubak, granted in old age,
Look, oh my people,
My little one who will destroy the governors!
The hour of my wish's fulfillment has come.
From God Most High,
This was what I had asked.
If you find an enemy to fight,
Let us go forth in support.
You have spoken true and worthy words;
Let us receive them and listen.
You began to speak quietly;
The youngest of the six lions,
God's beloved mortal,
The generous prince Manas—
You have just named him.
Let a son be unruly;
If he is not unruly, let him be nothing!
If your father Baltay does not die this year,
If he does not see the other world,
I shall make the stars in heaven pale;
To lion prince Manas
I shall make you a friend beyond this world.
If I do not braid the camel's tail,
Saying, ‘Here is your companion for life,’
To that peerless, bloodthirsty one,
If I do not give you as his companion,
Then I, Baltay,
May I never see Judgment Day!
God has brought me to my heart's desire.
God Most High, without stint,
Has given me
The valiant child Chubak.
What you have said is true as well;
All you have said is true.
My darling foal,
My plane tree with its single root,
Whether I walk or stand, now
I shall pray for your life.
To raid Akbaltay,
Many jealous ones lie in wait;
Many Chinese stand at my flank,
Many enemies seethe around me.
My son, the mountain horses are nine multitudes—
Warhorses and tireless racers together,
Let me gather them into a herd.
Collecting them in groups,
Let me send them past in a line.
A wondrous steed to ride in battle,
Leopard Chubak, my foal,
Let me find one perfectly suited!’
Giving orders to the Noygut,
Akbaltay began to speak:
‘The vast horse-herds in the mountains,
Drive them here without delay,’ he said,
And sent out the message.
Nine vast herds of horses in the mountains,
He gathered them without delay.
Driving them all in a tumult,
He sent them past in a line.
He had skilled men examine them,
Had horse-judges judge them.
Those damned horses,
He paraded them for forty-seven days.
Though they paraded, no horse was found;
Hero Chubak took offense.
He grew furious and roused himself.
His khan-father Akbaltay,
Looking at him, he spoke:
‘You have no beast to ride on campaign;
These horses of yours have no strength.
They have no mane or tail at all.
Calling it a horse, a mere black donkey,
You have reared a scrub-tailed thing.
Half a hoof and a scrawny neck,
You have reared a worthless nag!
Its pastern is four fingers long;
The whole of it worth one yearling,
You have reared a frog!
Its heel is one finger-width;
With no strength to carry a rider to war,
You have reared a pig.
In this matter, dear father,
You have proved a failure!
Without a wondrous steed beneath you,
You have no strength to scout,
Among your overflowing herds,
You have no beast to ride on a raid.
Wild asses roam the plain;
These horses offer no help.
Keeping useless livestock,
There is no miser like you.
Unable to choose a wondrous steed,
To bloodthirsty falcon Manas,
How shall I make my way?
Rather than this, dear father,
I shall go away to Mecca!
Gathering useless livestock,
Can a warrior be like you?
All your livestock, dear father,
Is it worth a single horse?
Useless, wretched livestock,
Can a man who keeps it prosper?
The four corners of the round world,
My prince and father, without relying on you,
I shall roam and search on foot.
If mighty Allah wills,
A wondrous steed to ride in battle,
I shall seek eagerly and find.
The four corners of the round world,
I shall search around them four times!’
Offended with his father,
Akbaltay's Chubak,
Who could throw the whole world into turmoil,
His reckless, ruthless son,
Would not cease seeking a horse.
His boiling fury seized him.
When he came on in desperate zeal,
Never turning back from fire,
Akbaltay's Chubak
Had imperiousness as well.
When a shouting tumult came,
He would not retreat from doom.
Saying, ‘I shall die in the end,’
He would not shrink from death.
The ablest of the tawny-gray ones,
Such was Chubak's nature,
Akbaltay's mighty one.
Thick-chested and broad-shouldered,
When advancing, never shrinking from the foe,
Set upon stone, never slipping,
Never turning back from embers.
Shrill battle cries and piercing shouts,
Dark resolve and stone-hard courage,
Akbaltay's valiant one.
With his father, deeply,
It seems he had taken offense.
Taking a bridle, walking on foot,
His thoughts scattered and troubled,
Khan Baltay's vast wealth of livestock,
To the valiant one born a leopard,
Looked worthless in his eyes.
Seeking a wondrous steed, inspecting livestock,
Your lion, falcon Chubak,
Left the Noygut without lingering.
Looking for a horse to ride in battle,
He left without looking back at the Noygut.
His mad disposition, his great fury,
Your formidable Chubak unleashed.
Deeply offended with Baltay,
He left the Oygut people.
There came a moonless, dark night;
To his mind, a day of turmoil came.
Seeking a wondrous steed, hero Chubak
Never rested for a day,
Never counted the days,
Never rested for a month,
Never counted the months.
Scattering much of his vast wealth,
Walking on foot across the yellow plain.
Day and night, for many days,
His thoughts filled, his mind grew aware.
Akbaltay's Chubak
Came upon the open plain,
At Baabedin's shrine,
At the source of a bubbling spring,
At the very plane tree.
It was an unpeopled, open land.
When he looked carefully,
They called it the Mediyen desert.
At the shrine's mysterious spring,
Warrior Chubak now made camp.
Resting upon his elbow,
Taking a short doze,
His closed eyes did not open.
Akbaltay's Chubak's
Outstretched legs did not draw back.
Pillowing his head upon the cloth bridle,
With his head toward the direction of prayer,
Akbaltay's hero Chubak,
They say, sank into a giant's sleep.
When hero Chubak slept,
Snoring deeply, heedless,
‘Someone may do me harm,’
He did not reckon it worth a trouser-leg.
Heroism and lion-like valor,
Allah Most High to Chubak
Had given beyond measure!
Wolf-maned champion Chubak,
Did you see what a support he was?
Born greater than mortals,
Did you see what a lion he was?
Lion Chubak then,
Turning himself toward sleep,
Every concern came to mind.
Devastating Chubak's
Heart burned with deep sorrow:
‘I, Chubak, who cannot reach a ridge,
Have come upon the Mediyen desert.
There is no yellow hilly pass,
And to be a companion at my side,
There is no hero equal to me.
The pine is alone, I am alone;
I have nowhere to turn.
To go on patrol and share my secrets,
I have no one to turn to.
Seen today, gone tomorrow,
Breaking people apart,
This wicked world brings grief!’
So said hero Chubak,
And sank into a deep sleep.
When Chubak went to sleep,
Taking a shortcut along a narrow path,
A horse was brought there,
Led by a man from the unseen.
Bringing it, that being
Turned the horse's head,
And to Akbaltay's Chubak
Stood calling loudly:
‘Turn your head toward us, my son;
Rise from your sleep, my son!
I am one from the unseen, here in the flesh;
I am the saintly elder himself.
Rise, my son, let me see your eyes.
The trust bestowed by Allah,
Let me deliver that trust.
Let me speak words of benefit.
A gray wondrous steed none could find,
I have brought before you;
Let me hand it over and return.
The horse I lead is Kögala;
Do not question this wondrous steed's worth.
He is the finest wondrous steed.
Allah Most High has allotted him to you;
This is the time he is given.
He has just reached five years old.
